# Gospel of Mary — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (attributed to Mary Magdalene as visionary, not author) |
| **Date** | c. 120–180 CE |
| **Audience** | Possibly communities in Syria or Egypt in the developing Gnostic tradition |
| **Genre** | Revelatory dialogue gospel / visionary ascent text |
| **Timeline** | Second century, during the great proliferation of alternative Christian writings |
| **In One Sentence** | A damaged, fragmentary gospel in which Mary Magdalene receives a private vision of the risen Jesus and describes the soul's ascent through hostile cosmic powers — only to face bitter resistance from Peter and Andrew, who refuse to believe a woman could receive revelation superior to theirs. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Gospel of Mary exists in two manuscripts, both fragmentary, and both significant. The primary text is in Coptic (P.Berol. 8502, the Berlin Codex, copied approximately the fifth century but based on an earlier Greek original), and two small Greek fragments (P.Oxy. 3525 and P.Ryl. 463) preserve parts of the Greek version from roughly the second or third century. The gospel is almost certainly a second-century composition. It was completely unknown to the modern world until 1896, when a Berlin antiquities dealer acquired the Berlin Codex, and it was not fully published until 1955.

The manuscript as we have it has devastating lacunae — gaps in the text where pages have been lost. The Berlin Codex is missing pages 1–6 and pages 11–14, meaning the beginning of the gospel and a crucial middle section are simply gone. What survives is about half the original text, and we must read it knowing that the full picture is permanently unavailable.

The world behind the text is one of intense early Christian debate about authority, revelation, gender, and the nature of salvation. Who speaks for Jesus after his death? The canonical answer — enshrined in Matthew 16, John 21, Acts 1, and 1 Corinthians 15 — is Peter and the Twelve (all male), whose authority rests on their historical companionship with Jesus and their witness to the resurrection. The Gospel of Mary offers a different answer: Mary Magdalene, who received a private post-resurrection vision that the male disciples did not share, has access to revelation they lack. The conflict this produces is the drama of the gospel's second half.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Gospel of Mary was written to make a claim: that authentic revelation is not constrained by gender, that Mary Magdalene's spiritual authority is genuine and divinely given, and that the male apostles who resist it are wrong — motivated by their own wounded pride rather than by sound theological reasoning. This is not a subtle argument. Peter's objection ("Did he really speak secretly with a woman and not openly to us? Are we to turn about and all listen to her? Did he prefer her to us?") and Andrew's ("I at least do not believe that the Savior said this. For certainly these teachings are strange ideas") are presented without sympathy. Levi's response — "Peter, you have always been hot-tempered. Now I see you contending against the woman like the adversaries. But if the Savior made her worthy, who are you indeed to reject her? Surely the Savior knows her very well" — is the theological verdict of the text.

The gospel also contains a genuine piece of Gnostic cosmology in its vision section: the soul's ascent through four powers (sometimes enumerated as the powers of Darkness, Desire, Ignorance, and Death/the Wrath of Death), each of which accosts the ascending soul and claims authority over it, each of which the soul refutes with a counter-argument. This ascent narrative is the theological heart of the text — a description of how the soul achieves liberation from the material world's governance and returns to its divine origin. Mary is the vehicle for this teaching because she is presented as the disciple who understood the inner, spiritual meaning of Jesus's teaching most perfectly.

---

## How to Read This Book

The gospel as we have it opens mid-sentence (pages 1–6 are lost). What we find when the text begins is the risen Jesus speaking with his disciples, comforting them and instructing them. His opening teaching concerns the nature of matter and sin — matter came into being through itself and will be dissolved back to itself; "there is no sin, but it is you who make sin when you do the things that are like the nature of adultery, which is called 'sin.'" This is not moral permissiveness — it is a Gnostic anthropology in which sin is not moral transgression against a law but the soul's entanglement with the material passions.

Jesus departs. The disciples are frightened and weeping — how are they to preach the gospel when the Son of Man himself was not spared? Mary stands up and comforts them. She turns their hearts toward the Good and reminds them of Jesus's love for them. Peter then asks her to tell them the words of Jesus that she knows which they do not — "you are the one who knows the Savior best of all."

Pages 11–14 (lost) contained Mary's vision itself — the account of her encounter with the risen Jesus. When the text resumes on page 15, she is recounting the vision: specifically, the soul's ascent through the four powers. The soul, confronting the first power (Darkness), answers: "I saw you. You did not see me, nor did you recognize me. I served you as a garment and you did not know me." Each confrontation follows this pattern: the soul's true nature was always invisible to the power, because the power only sees the bodily garment, not the luminous inner self.

After Mary finishes, Andrew and Peter object. Levi defends her. The gospel ends abruptly with Levi's words and the disciples going out to proclaim the gospel — a strikingly inconclusive ending that either reflects the text's fragmentary state or deliberately leaves the conflict open.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The conflict between Peter and Mary connects the Gospel of Mary to an entire network of early Christian texts. In the Gospel of Thomas (saying 114), Peter wants Mary expelled from the group. In Pistis Sophia (a Coptic Gnostic text), Peter repeatedly interrupts Mary and the women disciples, and Jesus repeatedly rebuffs him. In the Gospel of Philip, Mary is the companion (koinōnos) of the Savior, kissed on the (fragmentary — possibly face, mouth, or forehead) by him. In the canonical Gospels, Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the resurrection (John 20:11–18) — the "apostle to the apostles" in the patristic phrase — and Peter's response in John 20 and Luke 24:11 is skepticism. The non-canonical tradition is developing a sustained meditation on the theological implications of the canonical tradition's own account.

The soul's ascent through hostile powers connects the Gospel of Mary to a vast literature of Jewish and Christian mystical ascent texts: the Hekhalot literature, the Ascension of Isaiah, the Apocalypse of Paul, and Neoplatonic descriptions of the soul's journey through the planetary spheres. The specific structure — four powers, soul's self-defense, liberation — is characteristic of Sethian Gnostic cosmology, which also appears in the Apocryphon of John, the Gospel of Judas, and Zostrianos.

Levi's defense of Mary — "the Savior made her worthy" — connects to Paul's principle in Galatians 3:28 ("there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus") and to the broader early Christian debate about women's roles in leadership and prophetic ministry. The Gospel of Mary represents one side of this debate; 1 Timothy 2:12 ("I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man") represents the other.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand is that the conflict in this text is not primarily about gender in the modern feminist sense — it is about the nature of revelation and authority. Mary's claim is not simply "women can lead" but "my vision is genuine and authoritative." Peter's rejection is not primarily sexist prejudice (though the text certainly presents it as such) but a claim about proper channels of apostolic authority: Jesus taught his disciples publicly and collectively; private visionary experiences, especially those claiming to supersede public teaching, are suspect.

This is, in fact, a live debate in second-century Christianity. The Montanist movement (c. 170 CE and later) was centered on ecstatic prophecy received by two women (Priscilla and Maximilla) and their male companion Montanus, and it was energetically suppressed by what became orthodox Christianity. The Gospel of Mary, with its vindication of private female visionary revelation against the resistant male apostolic establishment, reads like a manifesto for exactly the kind of Christianity that was being suppressed.

The cosmology of the ascent vision will seem alien to readers formed by mainstream Christianity. The four powers that accost the ascending soul are not demonic in the Jewish sense — they are not fallen rebels but structural features of the cosmos, the governing principles of the material world. The soul's liberation is not moral (defeating temptation) but epistemological (demonstrating that its true self was never subject to these powers). This is Gnostic soteriology: salvation as awakening to one's true nature, not as forgiveness of transgression.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Gospel of Mary was never a serious candidate for canonical inclusion. It was associated from early on with Gnostic or heterodox Christian communities, its attribution to Mary Magdalene was never accepted as apostolic in the canonical sense (she was a witness to the resurrection but not one of the Twelve), and its cosmology and soteriology were incompatible with proto-orthodox theology.

The church fathers who mention a Gospel of Mary (Hippolytus, Epiphanius) do so in catalogues of heretical texts. The text was effectively lost to the Christian mainstream — surviving only in Egypt, far from the centers of canonical decision-making — until its rediscovery in 1896.

The text has received enormous popular attention since the late twentieth century, particularly in the context of discussions about Mary Magdalene's historical role and about women's leadership in early Christianity. Karen King's 2003 scholarly edition brought it to wide academic attention. Dan Brown's Da Vinci Code (2003) popularized a garbled version of its contents. Scholarly discussion of what the text actually says — as opposed to what it has been made to say in popular culture — remains vigorous and sometimes contentious.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 120–180 CE | Gospel of Mary composed (in Greek) |
| c. 200 CE | Greek fragments preserved (P.Oxy. 3525, P.Ryl. 463 date from this era) |
| c. 400–500 CE | Coptic translation made; bound into Berlin Codex |
| c. 1896 CE | Berlin Codex (P.Berol. 8502) purchased by Carl Reinhardt in Cairo |
| 1896–1955 CE | Manuscript studied but publication delayed by WWI, WWII, and scholarly disputes |
| 1955 CE | Full Coptic text published by Walter Till |
| 1945 CE | Nag Hammadi discovery (no Gospel of Mary, but related Gnostic texts) |
| 2003 CE | Karen King's The Gospel of Mary of Magdala brings text to wide attention |
| 2003 CE | Dan Brown's Da Vinci Code popularizes (and distorts) awareness of the text |
| 2012 CE | "Gospel of Jesus's Wife" fragment (later shown to be forgery) re-ignites interest |

---

*— HESED, Reader's Guide Division*
*AI Bible Translation Project, 2026*
